nameStory: This delicate wildflower gets its name from Nova Scotia, where it was first scientifically described and where much of its population lives. The 'false foxglove' part comes from its resemblance to true foxgloves, though it's actually in a completely different plant family and much smaller than those towering garden favorites.
description: Nova Scotia false foxglove is a slender annual wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with delicate pink to purple tubular flowers. It has a graceful, upright growth habit with narrow leaves and small flowers that bloom along the upper stems. This rare plant is one of New England's most geographically restricted species, found only in a small corner of coastal Maine.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple tubular flowers about half an inch long with five rounded petal lobes that flare out like a tiny trumpet. The flowers have a soft, papery texture and often have darker purple lines or spots inside the throat.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, linear leaves that are opposite on the stem and feel smooth to the touch. The leaves are bright green and quite small, giving the whole plant a delicate, wispy appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright annual that branches in the upper portion, creating an open, airy look. The whole plant has a fine texture and sways easily in coastal breezes.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small round capsules that split open to release tiny seeds. The capsules are about the size of a peppercorn and make a subtle rattling sound when dry and mature.

habitat: Found exclusively in coastal sandy soils, dunes, and salt-influenced areas in southeastern Maine. It grows in open, sunny spots often mixed with beach grasses and other salt-tolerant plants. This plant needs the specific conditions found in maritime environments and won't survive far from the ocean's influence.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of narrow leaves, often overlooked among beach grasses and other coastal vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from mid to late summer, typically July through August, when the delicate pink-purple flowers are most visible against the coastal landscape.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, turning brown and releasing seeds by early fall before the plant dies back completely.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible, as this annual plant completes its entire life cycle in one growing season.

funFact: This tiny wildflower is so rare and geographically restricted that it's been spotted only 7 times by naturalists in all of New England, making it rarer to encounter than some endangered animals!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other false foxgloves, especially slender false foxglove, but Nova Scotia false foxglove is found only in coastal Maine habitats while others grow inland. The coastal location is your best clue - if you're not near salt water in Maine, it's probably a different species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'false foxglove,' this plant is in the broomrape family, not the plantain family like true foxgloves. Many false foxgloves are actually parasitic on other plants' roots, though they still photosynthesize and appear green like normal plants.
compareHints: Compared to its false foxglove relatives, Nova Scotia false foxglove is distinguished mainly by its coastal habitat requirement and very limited range. Purple false foxglove is much more common and grows inland, while slender false foxglove has even tinier flowers and grows in drier, sandy soils away from salt influence.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple false foxglove is the most common and robust of the false foxgloves in New England, with larger flowers and broader leaves than slender false foxglove.
Among New England's false foxgloves, slender false foxglove has the thinnest, most thread-like leaves - much narrower than purple false foxglove's broader lance-shaped leaves.
Saltmarsh false foxglove is the only member of its genus that requires salty conditions - this habitat preference makes it the easiest false foxglove to identify.

Tenlobe false foxglove is distinguished from other New England false foxgloves primarily by its flower structure - it has ten corolla lobes versus five in most relatives, and tends to have more deeply divided, thread-like leaves than purple false foxglove.
Beach false foxglove differs from its relatives like purple false foxglove and slender false foxglove primarily by its coastal habitat and extremely narrow, thread-like leaves.
